t.chasma i ayub khazira@40.0,64.6:
North of Bukhara, the green irrigated oasis of the Zarafshan river spreads out in a patchwork of cotton fields, orchards, mulberry trees and villages, and the point named Chasma-i Ayub Khazira lies in this landscape, near the village of Khazara, between Vobkent and Gijduvon. Chashma-i Ayub, the spring of Job, is a name given to several holy springs in Central Asia, linked to the legend that the prophet Job struck the ground with his staff and water gushed forth in a time of drought. The most famous is in Bukhara itself, a mausoleum over a spring, and this site near Khazara may be another shrine of the same tradition, listed as part of the Silk Roads corridor of the Zarafshan valley. I cannot vouch for what stands there today.

The area was on the main caravan route between Bukhara and Samarkand, and the towns along it, such as Vobkent and Gijduvon, have their own monuments. Vobkent is known for a tall minaret from the late twelfth century, decorated with bands of patterned brickwork, a smaller cousin of the great Kalyan minaret in Bukhara. Gijduvon is famous for its pottery, with a tradition of ceramics in rich browns, yellows and greens, and a family workshop and museum where you can see how it is made.

The riding here is flat and hot, with straight roads across the oasis, lined with poplars and irrigation channels, and villages of mud-brick houses. Traffic includes cars, minibuses, donkey carts and bicycles, and road surfaces vary from good to poor. Police checkpoints are common, so keep your documents ready. Summer temperatures can exceed forty degrees, so spring and autumn, with mild temperatures and harvests, are much better times to ride.

Vobkent, about twelve kilometres away, has fuel, shops and simple restaurants, though petrol supply in Uzbekistan can be unreliable, as many vehicles run on gas, so fill up when you can. Bukhara, about forty kilometres away, has full services and one of the most beautiful old towns in Central Asia. Local food includes plov, the national rice dish cooked with meat, carrots and onions, samsa pastries baked in clay ovens, and green tea served everywhere.
t.vardanze settlement@40.2,64.4:
North of Bukhara the irrigated land eventually runs into the sand, and on that edge lies Vardanze, the ruins of an ancient city that was once the capital of a local principality in the Bukhara oasis. Its mound of collapsed mud-brick walls and citadel rises above the fields near Shofirkon, and archaeologists have traced its history back more than two thousand years. It flourished as a trading post on the Silk Road and later declined, partly because the desert advanced and the water supply failed, and its ruins are part of the Zarafshan-Karakum corridor listed by UNESCO in 2023.

The story of Vardanze is the story of the oasis itself: a constant battle between the river and the sand. Canals dug over centuries brought water from the Zarafshan to the fields, and when they were neglected or the river shifted, settlements were abandoned to the desert. Today the Kyzylkum stretches away to the north, a sea of dunes and scrub, and in the evening the wind whispers over the ruins. Nearby Gijduvan is famous for its ceramics, with brown and green glazed plates and bowls made by families of potters.

Riding in this part of Uzbekistan is mostly flat and straightforward, along roads that cut through fields and villages and out into the desert. The surfaces vary, with good tarmac on the main roads and potholes or gravel on the side roads, and the traffic is a mix of cars, trucks, carts and donkeys. The heat in summer is intense, so March to May and late September into November are the windows to aim for. Watch out for police checkpoints, and carry your documents at all times.

Shofirkon, seven kilometres off, has a filling station and a bazaar, and Bukhara, with its madrasas, domed trading halls and the great Kalon minaret, is about an hour south. Octane is the recurring headache in rural Uzbekistan, where most cars burn gas, so take good petrol wherever it is offered. In Gijduvan, potter families still turn out the ochre and green ceramics the town is known for, and their workshops welcome visitors. Roadside sellers in late summer offer melons and grapes of absurd sweetness, and the round bread from the clay tandyr ovens tastes best still warm.
t.vobkent minaret@40.0,64.5:
Vobkent's minaret is a tall brick finger rising out of a small Uzbek town on the edge of the Bukhara oasis. It was built in the late twelfth century, in the same tradition as the more famous Kalyan minaret in Bukhara, which it predates in style by a few years and rivals in elegance. Standing nearly forty metres high, it is made entirely of fired brick laid in bands of geometric patterns, with a tapering shaft and a lantern top. Up close, the craftsmanship is startling: no two courses seem quite the same.

The town of Vobkent itself, with about seventeen thousand people, is ordinary and busy in the best way, with a bazaar, tea houses and workshops. The district is known for ceramics, and in the local markets you can find bowls and plates glazed in cobalt and turquoise. There is fuel here, and food is the dependable Uzbek menu: plov, shashlik, flatbread from a clay oven, and endless green tea poured by whoever is nearest. Bukhara is about thirty kilometres away and makes a good base.

Riding in this part of Uzbekistan is flat and fast. The roads run straight through cotton fields, mulberry trees and irrigation canals, with the Kyzylkum desert never far off. Surfaces vary, so watch for patched sections and the odd bump where the earth has settled. Drivers can be unpredictable, overtaking where they should not. Further along the oasis the Varakhsha settlement, an ancient pre-Islamic site with a ruined palace, and the shrine of Bahouddin Naqshband, a major Sufi holy place, lie within easy reach.

Spring and autumn are the seasons to ride; summer afternoons can climb past forty degrees, when only the foolhardy are out. The best light on the minaret is just after sunrise or in the last hour before dusk, when the brick shifts from honey to rose. Dress modestly if you enter the mosque or mausoleum complexes nearby, and carry water. Locals will be curious about your bike and likely to offer tea, which is worth accepting.
t.khiva@41.4,60.4:
Khiva rises out of the desert like a stage set that someone forgot to take down. The walled inner town, Itchan Kala, is built of mud brick and glazed tile on the edge of the Kyzylkum and Karakum deserts, in the fertile oasis of Khorezm along the lower Amu Darya. Its sand-colored walls, about ten meters high, enclose a maze of lanes, madrasas, mosques and minarets that was inscribed by UNESCO in 1990, among the first sites in Uzbekistan to be listed. Khiva was for centuries a khanate famous for its slave market and for the raiding caravans that crossed the steppe, and it kept its independence until the Russians took it in 1873.

The sights are close together and best done on foot. The Kalta Minor minaret, stubby and covered in turquoise tile, was meant to be the tallest in Central Asia and was left unfinished when its builder died, so it stops at a few dozen meters like a fat blue stump. The Juma Mosque has a forest of carved wooden columns, over two hundred of them, some said to be a thousand years old, holding up a roof that lets in only a little light. The Islam Khodja minaret, striped in red and blue, offers a view across the roofs. Climb it at sunset, when the walls turn amber and the swallows come out.

The road here is the real subject for a rider. From Samarkand you ride west to Bukhara, then north-west across the Kyzylkum desert for several hundred kilometers of long, dead straight asphalt with shimmering horizons and a few tea houses. The surface is mixed, with sections of broken pavement and sand drifts that make it tiring, and in summer the heat is severe, often well above forty degrees. Spring and autumn are far better. Wind can be strong and the dust thick.

Fuel is the practical matter. Gas for cars is widespread, but petrol is not always available along the desert road, and quality varies, so carry a reserve and fill whenever you can. Khiva itself has stations on the outskirts, and the hotels inside the old walls are small guesthouses with courtyards and breakfasts of bread, melon, yoghurt and tea. Khorezm melons are famous, so buy one when they are in season.

Eat plov, the rice dish of the region, and watch the sunset from the walls. The town is quiet in the evening once the day-trippers leave.
